title: TB5-05408
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), who is a citizen of Colombia, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), who is a citizen of Colombia, is appealing the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection. He has not submitted any new evidence in support of his appeal, nor has he requested an oral hearing. He is, however, requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) find him to be a Convention refugee, or in the alternative, that the matter be remitted to the RPD for re-determination by a newly-constituted panel. The Minister intervened in accordance with IRPA subsections 171(a.4) and 272(a.5) as well as rule 4 of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules. However, the Minister is not relying on documentary evidence referred to in IRPA s. 110(3), nor is he requesting that a hearing be held under IRPA s. 110(6).
Pursuant to s. 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Divisions (RAD) refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.

The Appellant is a citizen of Colombia, who has been a member of the Liberal Party of Colombia since 1982. He was an elected XXXX XXXX from the early 1990s to 2000, then from XXXX2008 until XXXX XXXX, 2011. Between the years 2000 and 2008, the Appellant was involved in politics as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in the municipality of XXXX and in the Department of Caldas.

The Appellant alleges that due to his involvement in politics, he was targeted by the FARC (Fuerzas Armadas Revolucionarias de Colombia). In 2000, the FARC forced the Appellant to pay them "protection" money. In XXXX 2004, the Appellant's son, when he became aware of the protection money, contacted the police and an operation was set up to apprehend the FARC. This police operation was successful. The guerilla member was caught, tried in court and sentenced to prison; however, he was released around XXXX 2008.

In 2008, the Appellant was again elected to the XXXX XXXX. However, due to death threats, the police assigned a bodyguard to protect him. In XXXX 2008, the Appellant's wife and one of his daughters left Colombia and their refugee claims in Canada were accepted on March 3, 2009. They applied for permanent residence and the Appellant was included in this application. However, the Appellant was refused due to "perjury".

Between 2011 and 2013, the Appellant was ill and was receiving cancer treatment, rarely going out onto the streets. However by early 2013, the threats from FARC began again. As a result, the Appellant left Colombia on XXXX XXXX, 2013 and arrived in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He submitted a refugee claim in April 2014.

The RAD has taken guidance from the Federal Court in Huruglica,1 (as submitted by counsel) wherein Justice Phelan states, in paragraphs 54 and 55, of the foregoing decision. 54. Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. 55. In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error."

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard of review to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau in Alyafi2 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decision has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada. The RAD has applied the reasoning as set out in Huruglica.3 SUBMISSIONS BY COUNSEL * Did the RPD err in its refusal based on the issue of subjective fear, which included "re-availment", Appellant's wife's return to Colombia, "delay in leaving", and "delay in claiming" * Did the RPD err in its section 97 analysis of the claim? Re-availment

The RPD noted that as a result of the Appellant's fears of the FARC, while he was in the United States in 2007, he and his wife applied for visas to come to Canada in 2007. When these visas were refused, the Appellant chose to return to Colombia, rather than seek protection in the United States (U.S.) or seek other means of attempting to enter Canada. The RPD acknowledged the Appellant's passion about his profession and political career, however, in the RPD's opinion this was an insufficient reason for wanting to return to Colombia and face a risk from the FARC.

The RPD noted that after the Appellant's wife came to Canada and became a permanent resident and that she attempted to sponsor the Appellant in 2009. The RPD found that on the one hand, the Appellant was intending to rely on his wife's sponsorship to come to Canada, however on the other hand he chose to remain in Colombia because of his political career, despite the risk. It was, however, acknowledged by the RPD that the appellant did have the benefit of police protection during this time.

The Appellant argues that the RPD did not accept that there was only one possible course of action by the Appellant.4 Secondly, the Appellant submits that the RPD ignored the Appellant's testimony that when he returned to Colombia in 2007, he took precautions to protect himself. Furthermore, the Appellant had police protection from XXXX 2008 until XXXX 2011 and was applying to come to Canada through his wife's immigration application. Thirdly, the Appellant submits that the RPD ignored the fact that the Appellant experienced threats from FARC even after he returned. Accordingly, it is submitted that the Appellant's subjective fear should not be impugned when there was an intervening period of 7 years between his return to Colombia and his refugee claim; considering he experienced risk throughout those 7 years. Lastly, the Appellant submits that the RPD made no general finding of a lack of credibility.

The RAD concludes that the foregoing findings by the RPD are not sustainable. The RAD finds that the argument with respect to the Appellant's career is quite plausible. After reviewing the transcript, the RAD accepts that the Appellant was passionate when it came to his political career. In fact, the RAD accepts all of the Appellant's arguments with respect to re-availment, and notes, in particular, the period of time when the Appellant had police protection. Wife's return to Colombia

The RPD did not accept counsel's submission that the Appellant's wife's risk was diminished because the Appellant was no long an active politician. It did not accept this because the Appellant alleged he was at risk, notwithstanding the fact that he was no longer an active politician. According to the Appellant, his wife was in Colombia as she misses her children and grandchildren. Since the Appellant's wife's claim was based entirely on the Appellant's allegations of risk, the RPD did not accept the foregoing rationale for being in Colombia as being consistent with a fear of harm.

The Appellant submits that the state of mind of his wife is irrelevant to the subjective basis of the Appellant. It is argued that if one indeed wishes to assess the wife's state of mind, then one needs to consider that "she moves from one house to another" and she returned under the bonds of family loyalty to be with her son and grandchildren. Furthermore, the Appellant argues that he was being targeted with or without continued political activity, whether in or out of office. Moreover, the Appellant submits that his wife is in Colombia without him; he is in Canada, and therefore, it begs the question as to why his wife would be targeted.

The RAD finds that a mother's bond to her children and grandchildren cannot be underestimated. Moreover, the RAD finds that the risk to the Appellant's wife, particularly when her husband is in Canada, is insufficient in the RAD's opinion to draw a negative inference or to make a finding that the Appellant lacks subjective fear. Accordingly, the RAD concludes that this finding is unsustainable. Delay in leaving

The RPD accepted the fact that the Appellant was unable to leave Colombia from the end of 2011 until XXXX 2013 as a result of having cancer treatment. The RPD also accepted that the risk to the Appellant would diminish during the time that he benefited from police protection from 2008 until 2011. Since the Appellant had testified that he had received a phone call which was the impetus for leaving in early 2013, he was asked why he had waited until XXXX to depart from Colombia.

The Appellant submits that it is trite to say that a delay in leaving the country is a determinative or decisive factor in making a refugee claim. Moreover, it is argued that since the Appellant was a dedicated politician who had been tied to his community over years and years of service, that he would not simply leave the country as soon as possible.

While the Appellant did not provide an explanation for this delay, the RAD finds that, given the Appellant's profile in the community, a delay of approximately 6 months is plausible and ought not to lead to a lack of subjective fear. Delay in claiming

The RPD noted that the Appellant arrived in Canada in XXXX 2013, and waited until XXXX 2014 to file a refugee claim. The RPD did not accept the Appellant's explanation that he was waiting to see if things would change in terms of being able to obtain police protection because of the length of time that had elapsed since he had received that protection. The RPD found that if there was a possibility of obtaining police protection in Colombia, the Appellant would not have left. The RPD also noted that the Appellant testified that it took time to obtain documents in Colombia, however, it did not accept this argument since the Appellant had allegedly been facing risk of death from FARC for a very long time.
The Appellant submits that he had engaged a consultant at least by XXXX 2013 to assist him with his refugee claim and that he had started to complete his papers in XXXX 2014.
On this issue, the RAD concurs with the RPD that "delay in claiming" indicates a lack of subjective fear and undermines the Appellant's credibility.

This aspect of the claimant's conduct is inconsistent with a person living in fear of persecution in their country. It is to be expected that genuine Convention refugees would seek protection as soon as is practical, once out of reach of their oppressors. The RAD is mindful, then, that one of the significant factors which speaks to subjective fear and credibility is the element of delay. Delay, in and of itself, is not normally a factor in refugee determination.5 However, it can be relevant and a potentially important consideration to the Board6 where the Appellant has delayed in making a claim upon their arrival to Canada and failed to offer a reasonable explanation for the delay.

In the particular circumstances of this claim, the RAD concurs with the RPD that the Appellant had an abundance of time to put together his documents, either before or after his arrival in Canada. The RAD does not accept the Appellant's explanation for the delay and finds that it undermines his credibility. Conclusions on subjective fear:

The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it made no general finding of a lack of credibility and frames its determination as a subjective fear issue.7 Moreover, counsel submits that if the explanations for the lack of subjective fear are reasonable within the context of the Appellant's particular circumstances, a conclusion that there is no subjective fear is an error.8 The Appellant's consistent evidence was that he was being threatened by the FARC and that he feared for his safety. It is argued by the Appellant that the explanations provided to the RPD were not rejected as being not credible and therefore, it had no basis to conclude that he lacked a subjective fear.

The RAD concurs with the Appellant that the RPD made no general finding of a lack of credibility and instead relied on determining the claim on the basis of lack of subjective fear. The RAD finds that the decision on this basis cannot stand for the following reasons: Firstly, the RAD has found that three of the four subjective fear findings are unsustainable. More importantly, however, the RAD finds that the RPD erred when it found the Appellant to be credible on one hand, and on the other, made its determination based on lack of subjective fear. Section 97 analysis

It is submitted by the Appellant that the RPD failed to conduct a proper section 97 analysis. It is argued that the RPD committed two errors in its section 97 analysis. Firstly, it is submitted that the RPD engaged in a perfunctory reference to section 97 and ignored or misinterpreted evidence. Secondly, it is argued that the country condition documents were sufficient to establish a link between the Appellant and his exposure to risk of section 97 harms.9 Moreover, the RPD accepted that the Appellant was at risk and acknowledged that the police had provided him with protection, his position as a former XXXX XXXX demonstrated that the Appellant had a strong connection with the government authorities.

It is submitted by the Appellant that the RPD committed an error in its section 97 analysis when it applied the wrong test to the Appellant's situation, when it referred to the current interest in the Appellant as opposed to the prospective test.
Since the RAD has found that the subjective fear findings of the RPD are in error, it is not necessary to conduct a further analysis of this claim.

Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(c) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the Refugee Appeal Divisions (RAD) refers the matter to the RPD for re-determination by a differently-constituted panel.
